If you want old school, beat your head in MeloDeath, this is your album. Their conviction is well placed, and they don’t make any excuses for it. As a long time fan of the genre, however, I like a little more variety in my daily routine. Aura of Decay Extol Many of the songs are on the shorter side, but that’s because they are so densely composed and packed, if they lasted longer, they might implode. The technical and progressive side of the band is vastly impressive…they have a command of these elements that few others do. But on the other side of the coin comes melodies that feel warm, inviting, even comforting. The fact that EXTOL can make one side play in the same sandbox as the other is really the key to their sound, and 13 years later, they picked up right where they left off. Shores of Hateg Oxalaia I especially like the technique used in the production especially. It’s grainy…opaque…even dirty, and it keeps a level of darkness throughout the album that fights with the light and hope of melody. The album is a wonderful example of the power of blackgaze…of how rage and beauty can coexist within the same space. Artifacts of a Bygone Era Illyria This was truly an outstanding album. Not only did the band continually balance two opposing forces, but the peaks that the songs reached along the way were completely organic and natural. It’s the flow here that is the album’s greatest strength. As beautiful as it is ugly, it’s as if one side can’t exist without the other. Trinitas Nova Spei Interesting example of having the right ingredients, the experience and recognizable veterans, with promising young talent and the ability to use the French language to it's best use and they don't stray away from making something that matters. Widerschein Abrogation Abrogation might be Germany's answer to the likes of Omnium Gatherum, Insomnium and Wolfheart, a hidden gem no less. Through Zero Elder Well this was quite the musical awakening....Elder might have taken the progressive rock crown off of Porcupine Tree and will wave the flag for years to come. Iñ Mongeletew Mawiza Let me be clear about something. It’s not a bad album, but it is just too far from the conventional definition of Metal for most Metalheads to really enjoy. It you like ethic music, and I hate to call it this, you might enjoy the sound here. As it is however, it’s just too far from what I think of when I hear the word music. Thriving Love Sex Machine This was an excellent album, and an uncommon take on the genre of Sludge. There were grooves mixed into the mud, and even some melodies, but those down-tempo, massive riffs really define the sound. It was filthy, black, and coating, to the point that you couldn’t even wash it off of you after listening. Der dunklen Tugenden. Echos Vimbulnatt “Der dunklen Tugenden. Echos” is a surprisingly compelling and complex album—still very heavy, but it certainly makes you think and feel. Spiritual Nullification Vaeovon This is the epitome of underground extreme metal. Primal and discordant but also well-constructed and cunning. Not for the feint-hearted, this one. A Gentle Glow Anne Tapt This wasn’t a bad album per se, but it just didn’t do much to separate itself from thousands of other black metal bands out there. The feelings that the composer wanted to impart were real, however, but some more originality would take the band further. Origins Altersoul This wasn’t a bad album by any stretch, but it just sounded like a group of musicians trying to find their bearings and their way. They have the Metal sound down well, now it’s just a matter of trying to capture what make their sound unique within the industry. Indigo Asia Any album with 16 songs usually has me running for the hills. But I kept an open mind and can honestly say that I enjoyed every one. Not only that, but the album also gave me a newfound appreciation for the band and a longing that I have missed following them since their debut all those years ago. “Indigo” is a classy album that sounds just like the next logical succession in the band’s inventory. Encased in Deathlike Layers Ophis This wasn’t your average Death/Doom album. The band alternated between tones of despair and tones of rage and even added in some clean passages. Some of the songs were truly hard as well…as hard as steel. These varying landscapes made for an immersive listening experience. Chaosmongers Nervochaos “Chaosmongers” maintains a consistent traditional Death Metal sound compared to previous albums. All tracks are raw, direct, and aggressive Roar Whiplash Roar” is a traditional Speed Metal album with plenty of classical Heavy Metal vibes and a few Thrash Metal twists The Spell of a New Dawn Fading Light First, consider that this entire album was created and performed by a single person. That is amazing to begin with. It’s not just your run of the mill Black Metal album either. Sure, the aggression is there that fans want, but the orchestral elements make the sound swell to massive heights at times and create a much richer listening experience. The songwriting is intelligent, and the music is immersive. Ben Webster :: Music For Loving (1955) Posted on November 17, 2026 November 16, 2026 Music for Loving (1955) contains some of Ben Webster’s most sophisticated and elegant work, and the larger arrangements avoid the pitfalls of the “jazz-with-strings” genre. Inspiration, Not Limitation :: The Residents’ Eskimo Journey Posted on November 17, 2026 November 16, 2026 Many people have seen the Residents, but few know what their members actually look like. The group has maintained anonymity for over 50 years, through hundreds of releases, concerts, books, films, and pretty much every other kind of media. Still, if you’ve heard of them, you probably know their signature look: tuxedo with top hat perched upon a helmet that resembles a big, veiny eyeball. But did you know the eyeball wasn’t always part of the Residents story? Bob Dylan :: The Rolling Thunder Revue: The 1976 Live Recordings Posted on November 16, 2026 November 15, 2026 We all need a hobby. Some people get into fantasy football. Lotti Tauber :: Concern and Simplicity Volume 1: Original Recordings, 1981–1986 Posted on November 16, 2026 November 15, 2026 Yet another stunning archival find from the Freedom to Spend label?! Every time this crew pops up, you ask yourself how they’ve somehow unearthed more astounding and unique gems from the past. But FT$ has that magic touch. Case in point: Concern and Simplicity Volume 1: Original Recordings, 1981–1986 , Freedom to Spend’s latest release. Made up of barely circulated material by the late Swiss pianist / composer Lottie Tauber, it’s a minimalist marvel, influenced by Satie, Glass and the I-Ching. Radio Free Aquarium Drunkard :: November 2026 Posted on November 15, 2026 November 13, 2026 Freeform transmissions from Radio Free Aquarium Drunkard on dublab. Airing every third Sunday of the month, RFAD on dublab features Tyler Wilcox bringing you two hours of sweet sounds old and new. This month, the first hour is an autumnal selection of classic britfolk instrumental situations. The second hour provides a small/awesome sampling of live performances drawn from the ongoing and immense Aadam Jacobs Archives project. Sunday, 4-6pm PT. Marshall Crenshaw :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview Posted on November 13, 2026 November 13, 2026 With his crystal clear voice and keen melodic sensibility, Marshall Crenshaw stands as one of the finest rock songwriters going. His latest collection, The Bootleg Sounds of Marshall Crenshaw: 1984-1987 , offers a peek into his process. Culled from his extensive archives, the record brings together unreleased demos, live cuts, and unheard studio recordings captured in the lead up to his third and fourth LPs, 1985’s Downtown and 1987’s Mary Jean & 9 Others . Full of scuffed up, lo-fi charm, it’s a testament to Crenshaw that even his rough drafts feel like brillant slices of pop rock. Habibi Funk 035 :: Beirut City Pop Posted on November 12, 2026 November 9, 2026 In a departure from the usual template of old photos of the artists, the cover of Habibi Funk’s latest reissue features an illustration by Beirut-born, Paris-based artist Raphaelle Macaron. Poolside beach chairs sit empty on the patio of a luxurious apartment complex at dusk, separated by red, rocky terrain from the city skyline in the background. Cool purples, pinks and blues saturate the scene in a clear nod to the style of Hiroshi Nagai, whose work graces the covers of Light in the Attic’s Pacific Breeze City Pop compilations of funk, soul and AOR from 1980’s Japan. But while the references in the album’s title and cover art lovingly highlight the parallels with the City Pop era, the contents of the album highlight the perpendiculars. Linus + Bonnie ‘Prince’ Billy :: The Outsider: The Music of Jules Decorte Posted on November 12, 2026 November 3, 2026 Three oddly-shaped pieces come together in the most natural way in this under-the-radar release from Bonnie ‘Prince’ Billy. The disc reconfigures the work of blind Dutch songwriter Jules de Corte, an outsider artist who wrote and recorded over 3,000 songs during his lifetime. This is not what you’d call a natural fit. De Corte’s songs are quick and witty and cerebral, more like cabaret or art song than BPB’s mournful Americana. Yet the two artists share an unconventional spirituality; there’s real searching in De Corte’s cleverly put together tunes. The Aquarium Drunkard Show: SIRIUS/XMU (7pm PST, Channel 35) Posted on November 11, 2026 November 11, 2026 Broadcasting from Copenhagen, Denmark — the Aquarium Drunkard Show on SIRIUS/XMU, channel 35. 7pm California time, Wednesdays. Between the visible and invisible. Pastoral electronics, kosmische, fractured psychedelia, bent frequencies. 34.1090° N, 118.2334° W Lex Walton :: Ultimate Love Forever Posted on November 11, 2026 November 11, 2026 Lex Walton makes swaggering, theatrical, large-scale rock – the spit and snarl of her vocals punk laced, the instrumental arrangements swelling to arena-rock proportions. Dan Boeckner, half of one of the last big emotive rock duos of the aughts and teens, produced Ultimate Love Forever , and it has, sonically at least, some of Wolf Parade’s unabashed romanticism. The content is lacerating, the mood nihilistic, but the music itself is all about the good time. It high-kicks and cake-walks and vibrates with theatrical music hall energies. Transmissions :: Adam Voith Posted on November 11, 2026 November 10, 2026 Our guest this week is author Adam Voith, whose new novel, RIYL , short for “Recommended If You Like,” is an at times thinly veiled memoir of the ’90s Christian punk and indie scene. With echoes of Get in the Van and Freaks and Geeks, RIYL threads that delicate needle of looking back at earnest teenage corn doggery with warts and all embarrassment, tempered by the type of affection that only time and distance allow all of us. It’s also frequently flat out hilarious.
